title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
Tesla's Autopilot system was active during a fatal crash in March 2024. The company initially claimed it did not have crash video data from the vehicle, but a hacker recovered the data through Tesla's bug bounty program, proving the information was retained on the vehicle. The jury found Tesla partially at fault and awarded $243 million in damages, a verdict upheld on appeal in February 2026.

This incident shows a failure in data management and transparency in a safety-critical system. A deployed autonomous driving feature operated without adequate accountability mechanisms to preserve and provide evidence when crashes occurred. Catching this would have required Tesla to maintain reliable access to and disclosure of crash data during litigation, rather than claiming unavailability.

It is not established whether the data loss was intentional, negligent, or systemic across Tesla vehicles, nor whether it affected other cases or investigations.

summary:
Tesla faced a major setback in a lawsuit involving a fatal crash when a Russian hacker recovered crash data that the company claimed it did not have. In March 2024, a Tesla with self-driving features hit a parked car, killing Naibel Benavides Leon and injuring Dillon Angulo. During the lawsuit, Tesla told the court that crash video data was unavailable, but a hacker working through Tesla's bug bounty program recovered the missing information and proved the company actually retained it. In August 2025, a jury found Tesla partially at fault, and the judge rejected Tesla's appeal in February 2026, resulting in a $243 million damage award.

The incident raises concerns about Tesla's upcoming Cybercab launch, a fully autonomous vehicle with no human controls. Beyond this case, Tesla vehicles with self-driving features have been involved in numerous crashes, with 207 recorded in May alone, the highest number recorded. Tesla also changed the names of its Autopilot and Full Self Driving features to clarify that human supervision is still required, suggesting transparency issues around the safety of its autonomous technology remain unresolved before the new autonomous vehicle rollout.
